title: Factorising: Common Brackets, Grouping and Factorising Fully
subject: Mathematics
subtopic: Common brackets, grouping and factorising fully

scenes.heading: Factorising Further
scenes.subheading: Grade 9 Mathematics · Factorisation and equations, part 1
scenes.narration: Welcome to part one of our Grade 9 series on factorisation and equations. In this lesson we factorise with a common bracket, by grouping, and we learn to factorise fully.

scenes.heading: A common bracket
scenes.narration: Factorise x times, a plus b, plus three times, a plus b. Both terms contain the bracket a plus b, so the whole bracket is a common factor. Take it out, and what is left is x plus three. The answer is a plus b, times x plus three.

scenes.heading: Switching a bracket around
scenes.narration: Factorise two times, x minus y, minus a times, y minus x. The brackets look different, but y minus x is the negative of x minus y. So minus a times, y minus x, becomes plus a times, x minus y. Now the bracket x minus y is common, and the answer is x minus y, times two plus a.

scenes.heading: Grouping in pairs
scenes.narration: Factorise a x, plus a y, plus three x, plus three y. There is no factor common to all four terms, so group them in pairs. From the first pair take out a, to get a times, x plus y. From the second pair take out three, to get three times, x plus y. Now x plus y is a common bracket. The answer is x plus y, times a plus three.

scenes.heading: Grouping with a negative
scenes.narration: Factorise p q, minus two p, minus five q, plus ten. From the first pair, take out p: p times, q minus two. From the second pair, take out negative five, so that the bracket matches: negative five times, q minus two. Check: negative five times negative two is plus ten. The answer is q minus two, times p minus five.

scenes.heading: Factorise fully
scenes.narration: Factorise fully, three x squared, minus six x, minus twenty four. First take out the common factor three: three times, x squared minus two x minus eight. The trinomial can be factorised too. We need two numbers with a product of negative eight and a sum of negative two: negative four and two. So the answer is three, times x minus four, times x plus two.

scenes.heading: Keep going until you cannot
scenes.narration: Factorise x to the four, minus sixteen. This is a difference of two squares: x squared minus four, times x squared plus four. But x squared minus four is also a difference of two squares, so it becomes x minus two, times x plus two. A sum of squares, like x squared plus four, does not factorise. So the full answer is x minus two, times x plus two, times x squared plus four.

scenes.heading: A checklist
bullets: Always take out a common factor first
Two terms: look for a difference of two squares
Three terms: look for a trinomial
Check every bracket to see if it factorises further
scenes.narration: Here is a checklist. Always take out a common factor first. Then count the terms. Two terms: look for a difference of two squares. Three terms: factorise the trinomial. Four terms: group them in pairs. Finally, check every bracket to see if it can be factorised further.
